summary:
South Gyeongsang province has no province-specific transgender incident, ordinance or enforcement finding in these sources, so a visitor is assessed against the national framework of the Republic of Korea, which applies across the province.

South Korea does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The armed forces are the exception: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, and the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023. Enforcement has been punitive and targeted; in 2017 the military criminally charged 32 personnel in what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap, and she died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available without a surgical prerequisite. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that gender change cannot be determined by surgery, that court guidelines requiring surgery are now reference rather than criteria, and that every person has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children may have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors.

Restroom access is a live legal question. On 22 July 2024 the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a 3 million won claim, holding that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights, and that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right; the plaintiff had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020. A 2021 Daegu District Court (Pohang branch) awarded 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink to manage this, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed, including a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school who reported holding it in and leaving school early.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot: in November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender gap in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, stating that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children; a landmark 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity.

Documented hostility concentrates at public events and in everyday life. At an Incheon Pride event about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants and organisers later filed charges against pastors while accusing police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. A 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year, and during the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, accompanied by rising doxing and online harassment.
tangentialFactors:
Every ruling and incident in these sources comes from elsewhere in the Republic of Korea: the restroom judgment from Seoul, the sex-change ruling from Yeongdong, the beauty-academy award from the Pohang branch of the Daegu District Court, and the Pride violence from Incheon and Busan. None is attributed to South Gyeongsang, so the province is scored on borrowed national evidence rather than a local record.

The wider environment is measured in survey data. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates, that 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma. A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people, which bears on how reliably a visitor can expect incidents to be reported. LGBTI organisations can register, but an NGO that won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 faced government appeals, part of what Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Outing risk extends beyond restrooms. Contact tracing during the May 2020 Itaewon cluster exposed LGBTQ people publicly, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.
localsOnly:
Residents of South Gyeongsang access legal gender recognition through the same national courts, and since 8 May 2024 surgery is no longer required for a registered-sex change; the Yeongdong court held that outdated judicial guidelines requiring surgery are reference material only. Recognition for transgender parents of minor children has been available since the Supreme Court's en banc ruling of 24 November 2022, conditional on the applicant being unmarried.

Residents of military age face a distinct set of rules: article 92-6 of the Military Criminal Act exposes consensual same-sex conduct between personnel to up to two years' imprisonment, while transgender people are excluded from service altogether. The treatment of Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su and the subsequent posthumous reinstatement and line-of-duty recognition are the documented reference points for how the armed forces handle a trans soldier.

Everyday infrastructure remains contested for residents. The state has been held liable for police advice restricting restroom use, beauty academies have been ordered to pay damages for barring a trans student, and the National Human Rights Commission's 2021 survey shows large numbers of transgender people restricting food, drink or restroom use as a result. Trans teenagers in the school system report the same avoidance at school, and the Ministry of Health and Welfare has declined to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients.

Residents have no comprehensive statutory protection: there is no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions, and no joint adoption for same-sex couples. Conversion therapy continues to be recommended to outed people in a substantial minority of cases, with high reported harm.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records an incident, ordinance, court ruling, police action or facility dispute originating in South Gyeongsang itself; the province-level position on restroom access, hospitalisation practice and local Pride events is not sourced either way.

Whether article 92-6 has been enforced against personnel stationed in the province is not sourced, and no figure is available for how many people in South Gyeongsang hold amended legal sex markers.

The inventory does not resolve whether the national hospitalisation-guideline refusal has produced concrete denials of care in the province, nor whether provincial schools have adopted the restroom reforms that researchers recommended after the DDing Dong findings.

It remains unresolved whether the appellate restroom judgment's holding on comfortable restroom use as a fundamental right has been applied to provincial facilities, since no follow-on case appears in these sources.
